note: Bridge claims Jackson Pollock's own description of his process never uses 'action painting,' the term Harold Rosenberg coined in 1952. Target confirms: Pollock's narration for Namuth's camera ('I don't work from drawings or color sketches...') never mentions performance or an arena, and the target states Rosenberg 'published "The American Action Painters" in ARTnews' in 'December 1952,' with 'Pollock's own description of his process... reads far more plainly' and never used the term himself.

Bridge claims Klimt's paintings are contested for entirely different reasons than Warhol's authentication dispute. Target confirms Klimt's disputes are restitution/ownership cases tied to Nazi looting: 'an Austrian arbitration award... sent five Nazi-looted Bloch-Bauer paintings to Maria Altmann's family' and the 2004 US Supreme Court case only decided Austria could be sued, not ownership -- categorically different from an authentication dispute over whether a work was validly produced under an artist's process.

Bridge claims the Kahlo market is 'small enough to keep attracting fakes.' Target's own title is literally 'Frida Kahlo's Paintings: How a Career This Small Keeps Attracting Fakes,' and its coreSummary documents three separate authentication disputes (2009 archive, 2019/2020 Wounded Table claims, October 2025 Bavarian forgery seizure) tied directly to the small size of her ~150-painting catalogue.

Bridge claims a 1967 critic said Convergence's reworked color clashed with the canvas, and the painting later became a 340-piece jigsaw marketed as the world's hardest. Target confirms: writing in 1967, curator William Rubin judged the reds have 'an unfortunate tendency to "pop" optically out of pictorial fabric' (i.e., clash), and in 1964 Springbok Editions released a '340-piece jigsaw puzzle' marketed with the tagline 'the world's most difficult puzzle.'
